title: Fractal Dimensions of Canada's Borders and Coastlines
content: This study establishes a systematic geometric characterization of Canada's boundaries and coastlines using an adaptive-scale, dual-method framework. Globally, Canada occupies the second-highest position among the thirty-one largest country landmasses, yielding a box-counting dimension of 1.1945 and a divider dimension of 1.2085. At the continental level, the results reveal a structured progression within North America, where Canada's boundary complexity exceeds that of the mainland United States but remains below the highly irregular margins of Danish Greenland. National decomposition uncovers a pronounced hierarchy of intricacy: for the international terrestrial borders, the results show average box-counting and divider dimensions of 1.0193 and 1.0268, respectively, whereas maritime sectors exhibit significantly higher spatial occupancy. The Pacific Coast emerges as the most irregular national segment with a divider dimension of 1.4459, while Baffin Island yields the highest island box-counting dimension of 1.3156. By integrating these multi-level estimations, the research situates Canada at the upper extreme of the global boundary-complexity distribution, demonstrating that its national-scale geometry is a composite of smooth political frontiers and high-occupancy maritime margins within the broader global cartographic context.
